items.scene: Nina heard the new locker code on Monday. On Tuesday, she cannot repeat the code when asked.
items.question: What does this most directly test?
options: Whether Nina believes the code is false now
Whether the heard code is still retained in memory
Whether Nina was paying attention to the speaker
Whether Nina knows what a locker code is
items.why_this_case_matters: Prior exposure is established, and the task asks about current recall, so this is a direct memory-retention case.

items.scene: Omar was in the room when the teacher wrote a number on the board, but he spent the whole time texting and never looked up. Later he cannot repeat the number.
items.question: What is the best explanation for the failure?
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a common shortcut trap: the detail was never properly noticed, so it should not be scored as forgetting.

items.scene: Leah never saw the ingredient list. After tasting the soup, she says, 'I think it has garlic.'
items.question: What skill best fits this case?
items.why_this_case_matters: There is no prior-memory test here; the statement is a present belief, not recall.

items.scene: Mina saw a red umbrella on Monday. On Thursday she says it was blue because the umbrella now reminds her of a friend's blue coat.
items.question: What kind of memory error is this?
items.why_this_case_matters: She had prior exposure, but the current memory has been distorted by reconstruction and mistaken association.
